backups.overview: A remote, seldom-visited summit on the divide between the Cascade Pass and Dome Peak country, Lizard Mountain rises above the White Rock Lakes basin along the classic Ptarmigan Traverse -- one of the North Cascades' premier glaciated high routes. Most parties encounter it as a half-day side-scramble from a White Rock Lakes camp (reached via Lizard Pass), roughly three to four days into a north-to-south traverse from Cascade Pass; there is no dedicated trailhead or day-hike approach. The Class 3 heather-and-slab summit rewards the effort with sweeping views over the LeConte and South Cascade Glaciers (the latter a long-term USGS benchmark glacier used for decades of glacier mass-balance research) toward Dome Peak and Glacier Peak.
backups.beta: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own — parties reach it only by first completing several days of the Ptarmigan Traverse's off-trail, glaciated high route, then scrambling from a camp near Lizard Col. The summit push itself is straightforward (class 3) once you're on site; the real crux of the route is the multi-day glacier approach to get there.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround for the glacier crossings to and from Lizard Col: deteriorating weather or whiteout on the Le Conte or South Cascade Glaciers sharply raises crevasse-fall and navigation risk, and this is remote terrain where a late retreat can force an unplanned bivouac.
backups.face: South (county-line) ridge from the Sentinel Peak col
backups.comms: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent through most of this remote, glaciated section of the Glacier Peak Wilderness. NPS advises against relying on cell or satellite phones alone and recommends a two-way satellite messenger (e.g., a PLB or inReach) for this route.
backups.descent: Reverse the Class 3 scramble back down to Lizard Pass and the White Rock Lakes camp — there is no separate descent trail. From camp, retrace the way you came in: south past Spire Col and Cub Lake, then down Bachelor Creek to the Downey Creek trail and the trailhead. Parties who are instead walking the full Ptarmigan Traverse pick Lizard up mid-route and carry on to the other end, finishing at Cascade Pass rather than Downey Creek — that is a shuttle trip and a different outing from the approach described here.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead (Trail #768, Suiattle River Road)
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road, 23 mi from Marblemount; NW Forest Pass required and a self-issue wilderness permit is needed for any overnight camping beyond here.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Top of the maintained trail and start of cross-country travel; the Ptarmigan Traverse leaves the trail here, climbing south toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: From the road-end parking, the maintained trail switchbacks up through old-growth forest for about 3.7 miles, gaining roughly 1,800 ft to the pass. This is the last of the graded trail — everything beyond is cross-country.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Gap between Magic Mountain and Mix-up Peak reached via a roped crossing of Cache Glacier; historically holds steep snow requiring careful kick-stepping into early season.
waypoints.directions: At the pass pick up the climbers' path bearing south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse across the east flank of Mixup Peak on heather and snow, crossing a spur ridge, to reach the toe of the Cache Glacier near 6,000 ft; rope up for the glacier to the col, or take the loose gully on its left. Early season the Mixup traverse is snow-covered with a poor runout, and late in the year the col itself can moat out and become awkward to step onto.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine tarn on rock slabs about a mile SSE of Cache Col; the traverse's standard first camp, with limited flat tentsites.
waypoints.directions: From the col descend and traverse south-southeast for about a mile over rock and heather-covered benches. Keep the ice axe in hand — the steep heather is the real hazard on this leg, not the snow.

waypoints.name: Middle Cascade Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Roped glacier crossing near Spider-Formidable Col with reported open crevasses on the lower icefall; parties stay high on the less-broken upper glacier and rope up, especially in whiteout or late-season bare-ice conditions.
waypoints.directions: From the lake climb to the Red Ledge, an exposed traverse across a cliff band that is the route-finding crux of this section and holds snow and ice early in the season. Above it, work up and around onto the Middle Cascade Glacier and rope up before stepping on: the lower icefall is broken and open crevasses are reported, so stay high on the less-fractured upper glacier.

waypoints.name: Yang Yang Lakes
waypoints.note: Second traditional camp on the traverse, a pair of tarns below Le Conte Mountain; reliable water but exposed, breezy campsites on heather benches.
waypoints.directions: Climb the glacier to the low gap west of Spider Mountain, then descend steep snow and scree on the far side to the tarns. In whiteout this is easy ground to get wrong — the gap is the only obvious break in the ridge.

waypoints.name: White Rock Lakes
waypoints.note: Third camp, reached via the South Cascade Glacier col and Lizard Col; base camp for the optional Lizard Mountain side-scramble on a layover day.
waypoints.directions: Climb from the lakes toward Le Conte Mountain, cross the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, then traverse onto the South Cascade Glacier and cross it to the col at its head. Drop the steep slopes on the far side into the lake basin. Both glaciers are roped travel, and this is the longest and most sustained day on the traverse.

waypoints.name: Lizard Mountain
waypoints.note: Class 3 south-ridge scramble on somewhat loose rock from the White Rock Lakes camp; summit gives a close-up view of the Chikamin Glacier spilling off Dome Peak.
waypoints.directions: From camp climb back out of the basin and gain the peak's south ridge. It is short but the rock is blocky and loose, up to Class 3 — keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the class 3 scramble itself. The real gear need is standard summer glacier-travel kit for the approach: a rope per team, harness, crevasse-rescue hardware (prusik cords, pulley/ascender), ice axe, and crampons for crossing the Le Conte, South Cascade, and other glaciers between Cascade Pass and Lizard Col.
pro_tips: There's no dayhike trailhead for this peak -- plan it as a side-scramble from a White Rock Lakes camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse, not as a standalone objective.
Carry glacier travel and crevasse-rescue gear for the approach even though the summit scramble itself is only Class 3.
Check current Suiattle River Road status before planning a south-side exit via Downey Creek/Bachelor Creek -- it's been closed to vehicles at milepost 4 since 2025 flood damage.
watch_out: Snow lingering in the summit gullies into July can hide loose rock and make Class 3 moves icy -- carry an axe and know how to self-arrest.
The Bachelor Creek exit is brushy and only partially maintained beyond Cub Lake -- budget extra time if using it.
backups.pro_needs: Protection needs are almost entirely about the glacier approach rather than the summit scramble: a rope for each glacier-travel team, a full crevasse-rescue kit, and a helmet for rockfall/icefall exposure along the traverse.
backups.approach: Lizard Mountain has no dedicated trailhead — the accepted approach follows the southern leg of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor out of the Downey Creek Trailhead (~1,450 ft) on the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) east of Darrington. Take Downey Creek Trail #768, which enters Glacier Peak Wilderness within the first half-mile and climbs gently through old-growth forest, crossing several tributary creeks (can run high in early season) for about 6.6 miles to the Bachelor Creek Trail junction near 2,400 ft. Turn onto the Bachelor Creek climbers' path — unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown (expect to step over or crawl under numerous downed trees) plus a brushy alder/slide-alder band around 3,800–4,400 ft that becomes a real bushwhack when snow hasn't flattened it. The trail fords Bachelor Creek itself, which flows fast and cold with snowmelt in early-mid summer — scout for a log crossing or plan on wet feet. Above treeline the trail breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake (~5,340 ft), a reliable water source and common first camp. From Cub Lake, climb a steep, often snow-covered pitch onto Itswoot Ridge (~6,350 ft), another established camp with tarn water. Beyond Itswoot Ridge the route goes cross-country (boot path in season) toward and across South Cascade Glacier — a real glacier with crevasse hazard, especially late-season when snow bridges have opened up; rope travel is prudent unless the glacier is fully consolidated. This crossing tops out at Lizard Col (~6,798 ft), the broad notch on Lizard Mountain's south ridge overlooking White Rock Lakes to the southwest. Trailhead to Lizard Col is roughly 14–15 miles one-way with on the order of 5,000+ ft of net gain (more once the undulating up-and-over-Itswoot-Ridge terrain is counted), so almost everyone treats this as a 2–3 day round trip rather than a day climb — matching the ~29-mile (46.67 km) round-trip distance. From the col, the South Route gains Lizard Mountain's south ridge directly to the summit, a straightforward but loose Class 2 scramble of roughly 600 vertical feet, staying near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the south ridge scramble from the summit back down to Lizard Col — this is Class 2 the whole way with no rappelling required on the peak itself (rappels: 0). From the col, retrace the approach: back across South Cascade Glacier (same crevasse caution as the ascent) to Itswoot Ridge, down the steep pitch to Cub Lake, back down the loose, blowdown-choked Bachelor Creek climbers' path (re-fording Bachelor Creek), and out Downey Creek Trail #768 to the trailhead — the same 14–15 miles and net elevation loss as the approach. Because of the length, most parties descend only as far as camp at Itswoot Ridge or Cub Lake on summit day and walk out to the trailhead the following day. There is no shorter or technical alternate descent documented for this route; it is a walk/scramble-off, not a rappel route.
backups.bail: There is no quick bail option once committed past Cache Col — retreat means reversing the glaciated route back to the Cascade Pass Trailhead. Do not count on reaching the Downey Creek/Suiattle River Road exit, which is currently closed by flood damage.

pitch_detail.notes: County-line ridge from the Sentinel Peak-Lizard Mountain saddle (6,940 ft) to the summit (7,420 ft), ~480 ft of relief. Direct ridge crest is Class 3; an easier bypass traverses talus and duff benches on the west face.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP backcountry permits (Cascade Pass/Ptarmigan zone) are quota-limited and competitive in July-August; the traverse's glacier crossings usually aren't safely passable until mid-to-late July after snow consolidates.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or $30/year) required to park at the Downey Creek trailhead if using the south approach.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) inside Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft in wilderness.
access.permit: A North Cascades NP backcountry permit is required for the Cascade Pass portion of the approach ($10/person + $6 reservation fee via Recreation.gov, or free walk-up subject to availability at the Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount). No permit is required once you cross Cache Col into Glacier Peak Wilderness, though signing trail registers is requested.
access.closures: Suiattle River Road (FS-26) is closed to motor vehicles at milepost 4 due to 2025 atmospheric-river flood damage, under a closure order in effect April 2, 2026 - January 1, 2028; the Downey Creek trailhead beyond it is cut off by multiple washouts while the order stands, so do not plan an exit that depends on it.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, jointly administered by the Darrington Ranger District (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest) on the west/south approach and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest to the east; the northern approach via Cascade Pass and Cache Col lies within North Cascades National Park.

emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades NP Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount (north/Cascade Pass approach) or Darrington Ranger District, Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF (south/Suiattle River-Downey Creek approach) -- not the Chelan Ranger District, which sits on the opposite, east side of the range and is not the practical access point despite the Chelan County line running nearby.
emergency.nearestHospital: Harborview Medical Center, Seattle -- the regional Level I trauma center that receives most serious North Cascades climbing-accident evacuations by helicopter. Lake Chelan Community Hospital, while nominally in the same county, is a small critical-access facility on the far side of the range from every practical trailhead and is not the realistic evacuation destination.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Chelan County Sheriff's Office holds formal SAR jurisdiction (and operates its own helicopters), but since every practical trailhead is on the west side of the range, rescues are commonly coordinated with Skagit or Snohomish County SAR resources as well.

approach_variants.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
approach_variants.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
hazards: roped glacier travel on the Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers, with crevasses opening through late season
steep heather above the Cache Col descent, where a slip runs out onto rock
the Red Ledge can hold an open moat, verglas or fresh snow well into summer
whiteout navigation at the Spider-Formidable col, with no bail once past Cache Col
loose blocks on the summit ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. The notch you want is the broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. Standing in it, White Rock Lakes should be below you to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice below you to the northeast; the ground rising off the col toward the high point is a single broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, and the top of it is visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep going up, you are at the wrong gap in the ridge. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling on loose blocks — if you meet a step that makes you want a rope, you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, where the rubble is worst. Stay near the crest and keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

approach_variants.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek
approach_variants.notes: The other end of the same corridor, and the shorter way if Lizard is the objective rather than the traverse. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown — expect to step over and crawl under a great deal of it — with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt; scout for a log rather than committing to a wet crossing. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge, another established camp with tarn water, and from there the route goes cross-country across the South Cascade Glacier to top out at the col on Lizard's south ridge.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.

the Bachelor Creek ford during snowmelt
crevasse hazard on the South Cascade Glacier, worst late season once snow bridges have opened

approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. Coming up the South Cascade Glacier you top out in a broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. From it, White Rock Lakes lie below to the southwest and the glacier you just left lies below to the northeast; the ground rising toward the high point is one broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, with its top visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep gaining height, you are at the wrong gap. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling — a step that makes you want a rope means you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, which carry the worst of the rubble. Stay near the crest, and keep the party abreast rather than strung out directly below one another.

climbing_route.label: South ridge from Lizard Col
climbing_route.notes: From the col the South Route gains Lizard Mountain's south ridge directly to the summit, a straightforward but loose scramble of roughly 600 vertical feet; stay near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks.

bivy.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
bivy.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
bivy.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

backups.name: North Buttress
backups.fa: Fred Beckey & Mark Fielding, July 14-15, 1967 (upper buttress via glacier couloir; historically graded NCCS V, F8, A4 with 44 pitons and 1 bolt)
gear: rack to 3in with cams doubled on 0.5/0.75/1/2in
hazards: very remote committing position
loose rock on sections
long approach and descent
sustained exposure
backups.overview: Bear Mountain's North Buttress is a serious, remote alpine rock route deep in North Cascades National Park near the Canadian border, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Mark Fielding in July 1967 (originally rated NCCS V, F8, A4; now typically climbed free around 5.10). It offers sustained, high-quality climbing up the steep, glaciated buttress in an extremely committing setting near the head of the Chilliwack/Bear Creek drainage. Note: unlike some older references claim, this route is not part of Steve Roper and Allen Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs of North America list.
backups.beta: The most commonly climbed route on Bear Mountain's north face, established by Beckey and Fielding in 1967. The approach gains a glacier couloir on the west side of the north buttress. The upper buttress features seven roped pitches of excellent quality granitic rock with consistent protection. Route is usually climbed as a 2-3 day alpine adventure including a multi-day approach and descents.
backups.turnaround: Turn around if weather deteriorates significantly, if daylight remaining is less than 4 hours, or if any party member shows signs of severe altitude or exertion stress. This remote location has no rescue resources nearby.
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No cell service should be expected at any point on this route. Bear Mountain is a remote, roadless area within North Cascades National Park. Satellite communicators or emergency beacons are strongly recommended.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard (non-buttress) route, downclimbing a short 3rd-class gully; no rappels are required.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead (Trail 674)
waypoints.note: End of FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) off Mt. Baker Highway; Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk, and this is the start of the long multi-day approach toward Bear Creek.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Mount Baker Highway to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) and follow it to the road end at about 3,100 ft, where Hannegan Pass Trail #674 starts. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the kiosk here.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Broad meadow saddle where Hannegan Pass Trail meets the Chilliwack River Trail; leave the maintained tread here and drop north into the Chilliwack River valley toward Canada.
waypoints.directions: Follow Trail #674 up the valley, nearly level for the first mile and then at a steady grade, roughly 4 miles and 2,000 ft to the broad meadow saddle of the pass. Figure 2.5 to 3 hours.

waypoints.name: Bear Creek Camp (Chilliwack River Trail)
waypoints.note: Established camp at the Bear Creek confluence on the Chilliwack River Trail, the jump-off point for the Bear Mountain approach; NPS closed this camp after the 2021 Bear Creek Fire, so verify current access before counting on it.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the east side of the pass and continue about 5 miles down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the national park boundary where the Chilliwack River Trail proper begins. The tread loses elevation past U.S. Cabin camp to the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-cable car and a serious ford in high water, then runs down-valley past the Copper Creek and Brush Creek camps to the Bear Creek confluence, roughly 17 miles and 8 to 9 hours from the car. Check current status of the Bear Creek camp, which the Park Service closed after the 2021 fire.

waypoints.name: Meadows above Ruta Lake
waypoints.note: From Bear Creek, climb steep timber then huckleberry slopes east to treeline; the route gains the divide crest in open meadowland just above Ruta Lake.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at Bear Creek and ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing during snowmelt. Climb east into steep, brushy timber; higher the brush gives way to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows at about 5,800 ft above Ruta Lake.

waypoints.name: NW Ridge saddle high camp (6,480')
waypoints.note: Traverse loose south-facing slopes below Points 6592 and 6822, crossing a rock rib, to this saddle on Bear's NW ridge — the standard bivy for the North Buttress, roughly 9 hours from the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the divide from the meadows, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below Points 6592 and 6822 and crossing a rock rib, to the broad saddle at 6,480 ft on Bear's northwest ridge. This is the standard high camp, with running water and heather tent sites, and roughly 9 hours of walking from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Glacier couloir base below North Buttress
waypoints.note: About 1.5 hours below camp; loose rock and occasional icefall/rockfall off the shrinking glacier remnant in the couloir make early starts and helmets essential here.
waypoints.directions: The route begins by losing height: drop down steep scree trending climbers' right off the saddle and cross several minor gullies to the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the north buttress, about 60 to 90 minutes. An axe and crampons are worth their weight here even in summer. Loose rock and occasional icefall out of the shrinking glacier make an early start and helmets the norm.

waypoints.name: Bear Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit horn gained via seven pitches of 5.10 climbing up the buttress above the couloir; descend west on the south side of the crest, then downclimb a short 3rd-class gully back toward the saddle camp.
waypoints.directions: Climb the glacier or neve on the climber's-left side of the buttress and work into the slabs leading to the corner system where the technical climbing starts, watching for a moat where the snow meets rock. Seven pitches up to 5.10a follow the crest, with the off-width crux on pitch four and easier alternatives on the crest, to the top of the buttress; a scramble from there gains the true summit.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Chilliwack Lake trailhead, follow the Chilliwack River Trail roughly 6 miles (about 5 hours) to Bear Creek Camp at 2,300'. Just past Bear Creek, leave the trail and climb …
Descend a gully from camp to the toe of the North Buttress, then climb the glacier-couloir/buttress line to the summit before reversing the descent gully back to camp. This is the …
Reverse the Bear Creek High Route back down through timber and brush to Bear Creek Camp, then follow the Chilliwack River Trail out to the trailhead.

backups.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams from small (~0.4in) up to 3in max, DOUBLED on the 0.5in, 0.75in, 1in, and 2in sizes — this specific doubling comes directly from a route-focused trip report and gear list, not a generic guess. Bring a set of stoppers/nuts for thinner, more delicate placements on the 5.6-5.10a pitches. No pitons needed on modern ascents (historic 1960s FA account mentions pins, but current parties climb it clean).
what_to_bring: bivy/camping gear for the 2-3 day approach
food and fuel for a multi-day trip
water treatment (approach is via Chilliwack River Trail, largely unmaintained past the US/Canada border)
pro_tips: Treat this as a multi-day expedition given the approach
Strong route-finding and rappel management are essential
backups.pro_needs: Protection is generally adequate on the upper buttress's crack systems across the 7 pitches (5.6-5.10a); doubled mid-size cams (0.5-2in) cover the bulk of placements, with the 5.10a section being the crux and best-protected pitch. The approach glacier couloir below the buttress crest is loose, unprotectable 4th-class snow/rock/debris terrain with rockfall exposure — no gear is placed there, move efficiently and avoid lingering below parties.
backups.best_season: Mid-summer through early fall for the most stable rock and weather.
backups.aid_grade: A4 historically at the 1967 first ascent (44 pitons, 1 bolt, through an unprotectable overhanging crack); route is now climbed free
backups.approach: From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (~3,100 ft, end of Ruth Creek Rd/FR-32) follow Hannegan Pass Trail #674 — nearly level for the first mile, then a steady grade — about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Hannegan Pass (5,100 ft), roughly 2.5-3 hours. Drop off the back (east) side of the pass and continue about 5 more miles, bearing right at the North Cascades National Park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper; this section loses elevation into the valley, passes U.S. Cabin backcountry camp, and reaches the Chilliwack River crossing (historically a hand-cable car — verify current status with the NPS, since a high-water ford here is a real hazard). Continue down-valley past Copper Creek/Brush Creek camps to the Bear Creek confluence, roughly 17 miles and 8-9 hours from the trailhead including the pass. At Bear Creek, leave the maintained trail: ford Bear Creek (can be a genuine, sketchy crossing during snowmelt) and climb steep, brushy timber eastward. Above treeline the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake; from there traverse the divide, skirting the south slopes of Points 6592 and 6822 and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft — the standard high camp, with running water and heather tent sites. All told this is roughly 9-9.5 hours and 4,500+ ft of gain from the trailhead to camp, so most parties split it over two days. A shorter but more logistically complex alternative exists via Chilliwack Lake Road in BC (~9 miles to camp) but requires a border crossing/passport and follows an overgrown, unmaintained tread after the first 1.7 miles — most US-based parties use the Hannegan approach instead. From high camp, the route itself begins with a descent: drop down steep scree trending climbers' right off the saddle, cross several minor gullies, and reach the toe of the small glacier/névé spilling from the couloir below the North Buttress (about 60-90 minutes); crampons and an axe are genuinely useful here even in summer. Climb the glacier/névé on the climber's-left side of the buttress and work into slabs leading to the corner system that marks the start of the technical climbing, staying alert for a moat where the névé meets rock.
backups.descent_text: The standard descent off Bear Mountain's summit is a walk-off, not a rappel-mandatory line: traverse west/southwest staying on the south side of the summit crest, cross a notch/gap, and work across a snowfield that breaks the cliff bands above the Bear Creek drainage, then continue down easier 3rd-4th class terrain. A short, sometimes-loose 3rd class gully drops back down to the saddle camp at ~6,480 ft — about 1 hour and 1,400-1,500 ft of descent in good conditions. That said, this gully is exposed enough that a meaningful number of parties choose to back it up rather than down-climb it, especially with wet rock, a less-experienced partner, or an alpine-start-to-dusk timeline: a party that prefers not to downclimb it can rappel off natural anchors, though no rappel is required. There are no fixed bolted anchors on this remote, lightly-trafficked route — build natural anchors (horns, gear placements, slung blocks) and back up any old tat you find in place before weighting it. Below the gully, reverse the approach: regain the saddle, traverse back past Points 6822/6592 into the meadows above Ruta Lake, descend through brush and timber to re-ford Bear Creek, and rejoin the Chilliwack River Trail for the long hike back over Hannegan Pass to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Bailing from high on the buttress is serious; rappelling the route is difficult, so committing parties should be confident.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep corner just left of the crest; feels closer to 5.9+ with a heavy pack.
Fun, moderate climbing directly on the buttress crest.
Steep rock left of the crest to the ledge used by Beckey and Fielding as a bivy on the first ascent, leading into an off-width crack.
The technical crux: an off-width crack with surprisingly positive, crimpy holds; an easier 5.8 alternative exists via the buttress crest.
Blocks and cracks on the crest continuing to the base of a steep step.
Airy, exhilarating face climbing directly on the crest with perfectly positioned holds; an easier tension-traverse alternative exists.
Blocky climbing to the top of the buttress, from where it's a scramble to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Best climbed July-September once the Chilliwack River Trail and approach gullies are snow-free; the US-side trailhead is reached via Hannegan Pass or Chilliwack Lake Road (partly in BC), so check current border-crossing/trail-access conditions before going.

days.note: From the Chilliwack Lake trailhead, follow the Chilliwack River Trail roughly 6 miles (about 5 hours) to Bear Creek Camp at 2,300'. Just past Bear Creek, leave the trail and climb steep timber and huckleberry slopes on the unmarked 'Bear Creek High Route' past Ruta Lake to meadows on the NW ridge, then traverse below Points 6592 and 6822 to a good camping saddle at 6,480'.

backups.rope_note: Descent from the North Buttress (Beckey/Fielding 1967 route, aka 'North Face Buttress') is reported as a 3rd/4th class scramble/walk back to camp — no technical rappels are known on the standard descent, so a single 60m rope is standard; doubles/half ropes are unnecessary unless bailing mid-route.
backups.corrections: Existing gear text was flagged auto-generated/unverified. Verified against a route-specific trip report (Steph Abegg): the correct rack is doubles on 0.5, 0.75, 1, and 2in cams up to 3in max (not a vague 'rack to 3 inches' with no doubling detail), and the rope is a SINGLE 60m rope, not double/half ropes — descent is a 3rd/4th class walk/scramble back to camp with no technical rappels documented, so there is no reason to carry doubles. Also confirmed the approach 'glacier couloir' is loose, unprotectable 4th-class snow/rock/debris terrain (rockfall hazard, move fast) rather than crevassed glacier travel requiring a crevasse-rescue kit.
backups.rappel_count_note: No rappel is required: the short 3rd-class gully back to camp is normally downclimbed.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
hazards: a river crossing that depends on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread
loose south-facing traverse slopes below the divide points
rockfall and icefall out of the shrinking glacier in the couloir
a moat between neve and slab that worsens through the season
a position days from any road, on either side of the border
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS BY LOSING HEIGHT, AND THAT IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW AT CAMP. From the 6,480 ft saddle you drop down steep scree, trending climber's right, and cross several minor gullies to reach the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the buttress. ANY LINE THAT CLIMBS UPWARD FROM THE SADDLE TOWARD ROCK IS THE WRONG ONE.

IDENTIFY THE SADDLE FIRST: it is broad, it has running water on it and flat heather sites, and it sits on the north-west ridge with the wall around the corner rather than above you. A saddle with no water and no camping is not it.

AT THE ICE, THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE BUTTRESS YOU GO UP. This route climbs the glacier or neve on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress and then works into slabs that lead to a corner system - the corner is where the technical climbing starts. THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS ITSELF, WHERE THE ROCK MEETS THE ICE ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE, IS THE START OF THE DIRECT AND NOT OF THIS ROUTE. If you are roping up at the very bottom of the rock rather than walking past it on snow, you are on the harder line.

WATCH THE JOIN BETWEEN SNOW AND ROCK. A moat opens where the neve pulls away from the slabs and it deepens through the season; getting out of it onto the slabs is often the awkward move of the approach and it is worth an axe and crampons even in high summer.

A CROSS-CHECK ONCE COMMITTED: the climbing above the corner runs up to about 5.10 with the hardest move an offwidth part-way up, and it finishes on the buttress top, from where a scramble gains the true summit. If your first pitch off the ice is already at your limit, you have started too low and too far right.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It costs a legal border crossing, so passports and a plan for entering the country on foot are not optional, and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only with the paperwork in hand
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with the documents and permissions that implies
unmaintained and heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
the same loose divide traverse and the same glacier remnant beneath the buttress
a rescue that may involve two countries
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH VARIANT CHANGES ONLY HOW YOU ARRIVE AT THE 6,480 FT SADDLE. Once there, everything is as for the long approach: the camp is the broad saddle with running water and heather sites on the north-west ridge, and the route starts by DROPPING off it on steep scree, trending climber's right, across several minor gullies to the toe of the glacier remnant beneath the couloir.

THE SAME TWO TESTS APPLY AT THE ICE. Go up the snow on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress into the slabs and the corner system. If you are tying in at the very toe of the rock where it meets the ice on the right, you are under the Direct.

AND THE SAME NEGATIVE MARKER: gaining height straight from the saddle toward rock means you have not gone far enough down. The wall is below and around the corner from camp, not above it.

bivy.name: Meadow basin below the northwest-ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The standard and effectively the only high camp for the buttress, in heather meadow a little below the notch on the northwest ridge, where scattered trees give some wind shelter and flat grassy ground. Reached by climbing roughly 3,000 ft out of the Bear Creek valley to treeline on a rough climbers' path through open forest that gives way to blueberry brush. Around nine hours from the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side; the American approach over Hannegan Pass and down the Chilliwack River is far longer, on the order of seventeen miles, but is the one that keeps the permit straightforward. Expect mosquitoes.
bivy.water: Running water at the camp, fed by semi-permanent snowfields just above; those patches are described as holding meltwater well into the later part of the season.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, Bear Mountain cross-country zone: maximum party of six and six permits per night. This zone cannot be reserved in advance — it is walk-up only, from the Wilderness Information Center. Cross-country camping is restricted to durable ground.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count. The binding number is the permit: six people per party, six parties a night in the zone.

gear: full rack to BD #4 with doubles of mid-range cams
hazards: loose rock in sections
remote committing position

backups.overview: Bear Mountain's Direct North Buttress climbs the full buttress in one continuous push -- roughly 21 pitches of sustained crack and face climbing to 5.10-, first established by Alan Kearney and Bobby Knight over two and a half days in September 1980, and later freed by Bryan Burdo and Yann Merrand in 1985. Unlike the original 1967 Beckey-Fielding line, which reaches the upper buttress via a glacier couloir, the Direct start climbs the lower buttress from its toe, in the same remote, committing setting near the Canadian border in North Cascades National Park.
backups.beta: Established by Alan Kearney and Bobby Knight over 2.5 days in September 1980, the Direct North Buttress adds roughly seven difficult 5.10 pitches up the previously-unclimbed lower buttress before joining Beckey and Fielding's 1967 line on the upper buttress. Standout lower-buttress features include a 300-ft dihedral with a roof, a 130-ft hand-and-fist crack, and an off-width; the route finishes via the shared upper-buttress pitches to the crest.
backups.turnaround: Because the route is long (21 pitches) and rescue is far away, set a clear turnaround based on pace through the lower pitches to avoid finishing the upper buttress after dark or in worsening weather.
backups.rappels: None — walk-off descent, single rope sufficient
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage; a remote wilderness setting abutting the Canadian border.
backups.descent: Leave the rack and rope near the top of the route, solo easy terrain to the summit, then descend snow slopes through cliff bands back toward camp.

timing.recommendedStart: Alpine start from saddle camp; historically climbed over ~2.5 days including a bivy

backups.detailed_rack: Full rack from small nuts/finger-size cams up through a BD #4 (~4in) — the #4 is specifically noted as 'helpful on the lower crux.' Bring doubles of the mid-range cams (roughly 0.4-2in) to cover sustained, varied crack sizes across the route's 21 pitches, including the P3 5.10- roof and the awkward P16a 5.10- offwidth (harder with a loaded pack).
what_to_bring: lightweight ice axe (helpful for a steep snow section near the route base, not mandatory)
multi-day bivy/approach gear (2-3 day approach via the largely unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail past the US/Canada border)
extra water capacity (upper-pitch snowmelt is unreliable)
pro_tips: The lower seven 5.10 pitches are the technical crux — many parties still opt for the easier glacier-couloir start of the original route instead
Doubles in mid-size cams speed progress on the traversing, sparsely-protected pitches
backups.pro_needs: Protection is generally good throughout on solid Cascades rock, with doubled mid-size cams covering most placements and the BD #4 specifically useful low on the route. Watch the P6 leftward traverse past loose blocks — described as 'sketchy' and a real rockfall hazard, protect and communicate carefully there. Upper pitches can be wet from snowmelt depending on season.
backups.best_season: Mid-summer through early fall for the most stable rock and weather, matching the regional window for this peak.
backups.approach: Bear Mountain sits deep in the Chilliwack Range and is reached almost entirely on foot from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead: hike over Hannegan Pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail down-valley, then leave the maintained trail at the Bear Creek confluence and climb steep brushy timber to the meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide to a high camp on the broad saddle near 6,480 ft. The summit goes via the west ridge and upper north ridge (Class 4-5 scrambling) or the Northwest Ridge, the most commonly cited standard route. Round trips typically run 4-6 days with 30+ miles and well over 10,000 ft of gain.
backups.descent_text: Climbers typically leave their rack and rope near the top of the technical climbing, then solo easy terrain to Bear Mountain's summit before descending snow slopes through cliff bands back toward the high camp.
backups.bail: The lower seven pitches offer limited retreat with sparse protection; the easiest bail is before committing above the roof/dihedral section low on the route.

pitch_detail.notes: From the toe of the buttress, go right up slabs, then trend left into a broken slabby wall seamed with cracks. Climb the cracks to a recessed belay. The rock low on the buttress is poor in places; the couloir to the left is the loose, rockfall-prone alternative this start avoids.

Climb the crack in the dihedral to a roof. The crack widens toward the roof; stay in it until below the roof, then move out right, where a good hold helps. Pull through to a small ledge belay. A #4 cam is the piece that makes this pitch comfortable.
Continue up the corner system to the base of a chimney, then climb the chimney system; the two pitches can be linked. Stacked flakes lead into the chimney, so test before weighting.

Traverse left past loose blocks, which is the most unpleasant ground on the route, then back right through thin cracks with sparse protection. Ledge systems and easy but poorly protected ground follow. Protect the follower on the traverses and keep the rope clear of loose blocks.

Climb the ridge toward the snow patch; the rock here is often wet from melt. Beyond the snow, climb the face behind it by a left-hand crack to join the original 1967 North Buttress line. Crampons are recommended and a light axe helps for the snow.
A strenuous left-facing corner with a crack running from hands to fists, steep and sustained for much of a long pitch. The rock quality improves markedly from here up. Bring wide hand and fist sizes.
Two pitches up the buttress crest to the ledge at the base of the offwidth, where the 1967 party bivouacked.

16a climbs the offwidth, awkward with a pack, past some fixed gear; it is graded from 5.10a to 5.10-. 16b is the bypass: start up the offwidth, then trend right around the corner onto easier ground at about 5.8 and belay above the wide section.
Climb the buttress crest on steep, airy face holds with big exposure. Belay below the long crack system above.
A long series of thin cracks, close to a full rope length, to a small stance. The rock here is lichen-covered; expect it to feel harder when damp.

Easier blocky ground up the buttress to the ridgeline. Many parties leave the rope here and move up Class 4 and easy 5th, trending right to the summit ridge. Descend west on Class 3-4 ground, then snow and cliff bands back to camp.

backups.itinerary: Day 1: approach to saddle camp (~6,480 ft). Days 2-3: climb the 21-pitch buttress (historically done in about 2.5 days with a bivy), then descend to camp. Day 4: hike out.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-pulled cable car and a serious ford without it, then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since fire came through, so confirm rather than assume.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: a river crossing dependent on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber, slide alder, and a loose divide traverse
rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir
a deep moat at the toe of the buttress late in the season
sustained hard climbing days from the nearest road, with a descent onto the other side of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRECT STARTS AT THE VERY BOTTOM OF THE ROCK, AND THAT IS WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE ROUTE IT SHARES A CAMP WITH. From the saddle you first go DOWN: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS LIES ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THAT ICE, WHERE THE ROCK RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW. THAT JUNCTION IS THE START. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND IT IS THE COMMON MISTAKE: THE REGULAR NORTH BUTTRESS WALKS PAST THIS TOE AND CONTINUES UP THE GLACIER ON THE BUTTRESS'S CLIMBER'S-LEFT SIDE, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING ON SNOW WITH THE BUTTRESS RISING TO YOUR RIGHT, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE DIRECT AND ARE HEADING FOR THE REGULAR START. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A SECOND CHECK IS HOW SOON IT GETS HARD. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

WATCH THE MOAT AT THE JUNCTION. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, at the price of a legal border crossing on foot and an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
overgrown unmaintained tread
the same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall beneath the buttress
a cross-border rescue picture
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL DIFFERS, THE START DOES NOT. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

TIE IN AT THE TOE OF THE ROCK ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE ICE, WHERE THE BUTTRESS RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW AND THERE IS NO MORE SNOW ABOVE YOU. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

climbing_route.label: Lower buttress start
climbing_route.notes: The direct start takes the buttress head-on rather than escaping into the glacier couloir on the left, and that is the reason to be here: the couloir alternative is loose and largely unprotectable, with rockfall a repeated problem, while the buttress rock is clean and takes gear. Two slabby pitches on cracks around 5.8 lead to the crux roof at 5.10-. Grade V overall, about 2,200 ft and 21 pitches — this is a full day of climbing on top of a multi-day approach, so start early and know your bail options, which are poor.

climbing_route.label: Chimneys and rightward traverses
climbing_route.notes: Chimney systems above the roof lead into a series of traverses. The traversing pitches hold loose blocks and are the section most often called out as unpleasant: a block pulled here goes onto the belayer and onto anyone below, and traversing ground is also where a fall is worst for the follower. Extend runners, protect the second, and take care over what you weight.

climbing_route.label: Mid-buttress face climbing
climbing_route.notes: Face climbing and a left-hand crack system carry the route up the middle of the wall. This is where the rock can be wet from snowmelt draining the upper mountain — the same holds that are positive dry become slick, and the slabbier sequences are the ones that suffer. A cool, dry spell before the trip matters more here than on most Cascade rock.

climbing_route.label: Offwidth on the crest
climbing_route.notes: The buttress crest gives the second crux, an offwidth that is awkward with a pack on and has some fixed gear in it. A variation starts up the offwidth and then traverses right around the corner onto easier ground at about 5.8, belaying back at the top of the wide section — worth knowing about if the leader is climbing with a haul-free pack. A large cam (to about a 4) is the piece that makes the direct version comfortable.

climbing_route.label: Upper buttress to the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: Above the offwidth the crest continues at 5.9, then a long pitch of thin cracks around 5.10- to a small stance, and the remaining pitches ease off along the buttress to the ridgeline. From there most parties unrope and move together up fourth and easy fifth class ground, trending right, to gain the ridge that runs left to the summit. Rack: a full set of cams to a 4 with doubles in the mid sizes and plenty of slings; a single rope is enough because the descent is a walk-off. Descent goes west on third and fourth class terrain, roughly an hour, then down a short third-class gully to the north and through snow slopes and cliff bands back to camp — do this in daylight if at all possible, as the cliff bands are the part that goes wrong in the dark.

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
bivy.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
bivy.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

bivy.name: Boundary Camp
bivy.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
bivy.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

bivy.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
bivy.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.
bivy.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
bivy.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

backups.name: West Ridge (Beckey Route)
backups.fa: Fred Beckey and Helmy Beckey, June 21, 1941
hazards: Pervasively loose, rotten gneiss along the entire route — rockfall is the primary objective hazard
The exposed 'crumbly ledge' traverse below the Ridge of Gendarmes is loose and consequential
Redoubt Glacier crevasses open up as the season progresses — real glacier travel/crevasse-rescue gear is needed, not just a rope for show
Complex route-finding through the gendarmes and gully system on rotten rock — easy to get off-route
Extreme remoteness: multi-day approach on both the US and Canadian sides means any rescue or evacuation takes a long time
backups.overview: Southeast Mox Peak ("Hard Mox," 8,504 ft) is the true, higher summit of the Twin Spires and is generally regarded as the hardest peak on Washington's Bulger List (100 highest summits) and one of the state's "Difficult Ten." This standard route climbs from the Col of the Wild — the notch separating Hard Mox from Northwest/Easy Mox — over the Ridge of Gendarmes and up a loose gully system to a notch on the peak's west side, then three roped pitches (up to 5.5, easing to sparse-pro Class 4 near the top) to the summit. The peak's own west-ridge line was first climbed in 1941 by a Fred Beckey party; that route saw its first winter ascent in December 2023 (Eric Gilbertson and Nick Roy, 5 pitches WI2 M5 with rime-covered rock, ~18-hour summit push).
backups.beta: The standard/easiest way up Hard Mox: from a high camp near the Redoubt Glacier/Depot-Redoubt divide, traverse the glacier to the saddle between the Mox Peaks and Mt. Redoubt, descend into the 'Col of the Wild,' gain the Ridge of Gendarmes, then follow ledge/gully systems (West Ledges, Gendarme Notch, East Ledges, Southeast Gullies) to a high notch just left of the summit tower. From the notch, three pitches of loose 4th-to-low-5th-class climbing lead to the top. Per Beckey: most of the climbing is 'more intimidating than technically difficult; if a party finds the climbing above 5.5 they are probably off route.' The route is not sandbagged but is terrifically chossy.
backups.turnaround: Given the long glaciated approach, complex route-finding, and loose, exposed summit tower, parties should set a firm turnaround time based on remaining daylight and weather rather than push for the summit — the descent through the gully/ledge system and back across the glacier takes as long unroped-4th-class routefinding in the dark or in deteriorating weather significantly raises rockfall and routefinding risk.
backups.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels from the summit to the high notch; below it, one long double-rope rappel into the gully in typical snow-free conditions, or 6-7 improvised rappels/lowers (slung rock horns, knotted runners in cracks) down the gully and snow/talus when snow lingers
backups.face: West ridge / summit tower above the Col of the Wild
backups.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required for any overnight stay (reserve via Recreation.gov or obtain at the Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount) — per NPS's official backcountry permits page.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the remote Chilliwack/Redoubt Glacier basin; a satellite communicator (e.g., inReach) is strongly recommended and has been used to coordinate a real helicopter rescue from this route.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.
obj_haz: moats at glacier margins late season

waypoints.directions: This trailhead is on the Canadian side of the border: follow Chilliwack Lake Road in BC to the abandoned logging spur at Depot Creek, where the parking sits at roughly 2,350 ft. From there the approach walks the old roadway grade, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the Monument 65 border marker, where you cross into North Cascades National Park and should sign in at the wilderness-permit kiosk.

waypoints.name: Depot Creek Falls handline/cable step
waypoints.note: Class 3 scramble past a ~967-ft waterfall on wet, slippery rock; an old cable/handline aids a steep, misty 8-ft rock step.

waypoints.name: Ouzel Lake camp
waypoints.note: Flat sandy/gravelly moraine benches above the lake outlet; established high-camp for Chilliwack-range climbs, ~9+ hrs / 3,550 ft above the cars.

waypoints.name: Redoubt Glacier saddle / high camp
waypoints.note: Broken buttress SW of Ouzel Lake tops out on rock outcrops at this glacier-edge saddle; rope up here for crevassed glacier travel, visibility often poor.

waypoints.name: Col of the Wild
waypoints.note: Contour ~2 mi of moderately steep snow on the Redoubt Glacier to this col between the Mox Peaks; final ~100 ft is loose talus over sand.

waypoints.name: Gendarme notch below SE Mox
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 ledges and a Class 4 headwall gain the high notch on the west side of the summit tower; rock is notably loose with high exposure.

waypoints.name: Southeast Mox Peak (Hard Mox) summit
waypoints.note: Three pitches up to 5.5 (mostly Class 3-4 on the final pitch) above the notch to the true summit; descend by downclimbing/short-rappelling back to the notch.

backups.detailed_rack: Alpine rock rack with cams, nuts, and slings; bring a rope for the technical sections and rappel descent.
what_to_bring: Glacier travel kit (rope, harness, crevasse-rescue hardware) for the Redoubt Glacier crossing
A light rack to ~2in plus slings for the 3-pitch summit block
Sturdy approach shoes/light boots for the scrambling; rock shoes optional for the crux pitch
Passport/ID if approaching via the Canadian Depot Creek trailhead
4-6 days of food for the full approach-climb-exit round trip
pro_tips: Camp on the flat Redoubt Glacier bench (~7,300 ft) or the Depot–Redoubt Creek divide bivies to shorten summit day
Move early and be back across the glacier before afternoon sun softens snow bridges
Carry a topo or recent trip-report beta — the Ridge of Gendarmes/gully sequence has tripped up experienced parties
watch_out: Rotten rock throughout — test every hold and wear a helmet from the Col of the Wild to the summit and back
The crumbly-ledge traverse below the Ridge of Gendarmes is exposed and loose — many parties belay or rope up here even though it's 'only' Class 4
Redoubt Glacier crevasses open by mid-to-late summer — don't treat the glacier crossing as a casual walk
Route-finding through the gendarmes/gully sequence is notoriously easy to get wrong on featureless, rotten terrain
backups.pro_needs: Sustained exposed climbing to 5.6 on a long rib; a standard alpine rack and rope are needed for the crux and rappels.
backups.best_season: Climbable roughly mid-July through September once the Depot Creek/Redoubt Glacier approach and the summit rock are snow-free. The Redoubt Glacier's crevasses open progressively through the season, so early-season (late June–early July) attempts require solid glacier travel and crevasse-rescue skills, while late-season (late September on) parties should watch for new snow on the exposed rock pitches. A first winter ascent of the peak's west ridge (Dec 2023, Gilbertson/Roy) shows winter climbs are possible but demand a much higher level of commitment (mixed/ice gear, rime-covered rock, ~18-hour summit push).
backups.approach: From the Depot Creek trailhead parking on the abandoned logging spur off Chilliwack Lake Road (BC) at roughly 2,350 ft, hike the old roadway grade uphill (left-hand fork) for about a mile to the Monument 65 border marker, where you cross into North Cascades National Park and should sign in at the wilderness-permit kiosk. From there the route follows the unmaintained, unmarked 'Depot Creek climbers path' — a boot-track through old-growth forest for roughly 3 miles that gains to the base of Depot Creek Falls (about 4.8 hours and 1,600 ft in from the cars per one detailed trip log). The falls are one of the tallest in Washington (drop cited around 900-1,000 ft), and the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along its left edge; a fixed handline is present at the crux scramble section here and this is the approach's main technical hazard (exposed, greasy rock, worse in the wet or in the dark — several parties report losing the tread here at night). Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain, reaching treeline where climbers typically switch to mountaineering boots/crampons. Continue up class 3 tread gaining roughly 800 ft into the Redoubt Glacier basin; Ouzel Lake, in this basin, is the most common first camp. From Ouzel Lake most parties relocate camp 3-4 hours further up onto the Redoubt Glacier saddle/col (~7,150 ft) for a high camp closer to the peaks — this leg is flat glacier travel with only minor, usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions. From high camp, traverse roughly 2 miles east across snow/glacier beneath Easy Mox's south side toward the 'Col of the Wild,' the saddle between Easy and Hard (Southeast) Mox, finishing with a steep ~1,000 ft climb over notoriously unstable, sandy talus (loose rock is the dominant hazard on this whole upper approach — helmets on well before the col). From the Col of the Wild, ascend a ramp leading right past a snow patch into a gully, then scramble up and right (class 4, exposed enough that many parties belay it) toward a notch in the 'Ridge of Gendarmes.' A short sequence of ledges zig-zagging right-left-right leads through the notch; descend briefly to a small flat area and locate the correct gully leading to a high notch on the west ridge, which is the start of the roped climbing (two pitches of 5th class to the summit tower, then a final short, exposed class 3 scramble — stay roped — to the true summit). Water is available from the glacier/snowmelt and Ouzel Lake but not reliably along the upper ridge, so carry enough from camp.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent walk-off. From the true summit, most parties make three single-rope (30 m) rappels down the tower to a small, exposed high notch, then one longer double-rope (60 m) rappel from that notch down into the gully/glacier below — roughly four rappels in typical late-summer, snow-free conditions. Anchors along this line are almost entirely improvised rather than bolted: slung boulders, horns and pedestals wrapped with tat/cord, and the occasional jammed knot in a crack; a couple of the stations have accumulated enough old cord to look semi-permanent, but none should be trusted blindly and back-up/extend as needed. Bring a single 60 m rope (or two ropes if you want to do the notch-to-glacier drop as one clean pull rather than downclimbing part of it). In seasons or conditions where a snow finger lingers in the descent gully, parties have needed far more — up to 9-10 shorter single-rope rappels interspersed with downclimbing to get through the same 400-ft gully system, because a lingering snow patch prevents a clean full-length pull; budget extra time and a plan B if you find snow still choking the gully. Known hazards on this descent: persistently loose, choss-prone rock (the Southeast Spire's rock quality is poor, and at least one incident involved a slab breaking loose during rope retrieval at the notch and striking a climber), ropes getting stuck when pulled through the loose gully, high exposure along the east ledges near the Ridge of Gendarmes, and fatigue/darkness on the lower-angle terrain given how long this climb runs. After reaching the glacier below the Col of the Wild, reverse the approach traverse back to your high camp (Redoubt Col/Ouzel Lake), then descend the Depot Creek climbers path past the falls — using the fixed handline again on the steep slab section — back to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Bailing is serious given the remoteness; rappelling the route requires care.

pitch_detail.notes: From the high notch on the west ridge, climb a distinctive black-and-white mottled face (an FA-era account calls out a light-colored 'white column'/'brow' feature on this part of the tower) on rock that is surprisingly solid for this peak; low 5th class with deliberately placed, sparse gear, ending at a blocky horn rigged for rappel.

The route's technical crux: roughly 130-140 ft trending up and right past a white rock brow, curving left then back right above it. Exposure is sustained and the rock disconcertingly loose in spots, so protection is spaced and deliberate; the pitch ends at a solid horn anchor.

A blocky, loose rib leads up and across the summit ridge to the true summit; mostly class 3-4 scrambling but kept roped for the exposure, consistent with Beckey's own warning that anything harder than 5.5 here means you're off route.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN THE TWO MOX SUMMITS IS THE WHOLE NAVIGATION, AND THE TRAP IS THAT THERE ARE TWO SUMMITS. From high camp, traverse east across snow and glacier beneath the southern side of the western summit toward the saddle between the two peaks, finishing with a steep thousand-foot climb over notoriously unstable sandy talus - helmets on well before the col.

AT THE COL, CHECK WHICH TOWER YOU ARE UNDER. THIS ROUTE IS ON THE EASTERN SUMMIT, WHICH IS THE HARDER AND HIGHER OF THE PAIR. IF THE PEAK ABOVE YOU IS THE ONE YOU TRAVERSED BENEATH ON THE WAY IN, YOU ARE FACING THE WESTERN SUMMIT AND HAVE TURNED THE WRONG WAY OUT OF THE SADDLE.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE THE COL IS A LADDER OF SPECIFIC SHAPES, IN ORDER, AND IT IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE RIGHT: a ramp leading RIGHT past a snow patch into a gully; then class 4 scrambling up and right, exposed enough that many parties belay it, toward a notch in a ridge of gendarmes; then a short sequence of ledges that zig-zag right, left, right through that notch; then a brief DESCENT to a small flat area. THE FLAT SPOT AFTER A DOWNCLIMB IS THE CONFIRMATION - a line that only ever goes up has missed the notch.

FROM THAT FLAT AREA, LOCATE THE CORRECT GULLY LEADING TO A HIGH NOTCH ON THE WEST RIDGE. That notch is where the roped climbing starts: two pitches of fifth class to the summit tower, then a short exposed scramble, kept roped, to the top. IF YOU ARE UNCOILING A ROPE AT THE COL ITSELF, YOU ARE HUNDREDS OF FEET TOO LOW.

Carry water from camp. The glacier and the lake supply it below; the upper ridge does not.

approach_variants.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM EITHER CAMP THE ROUTE MEETS AT THE SAME PLACE: THE SADDLE BETWEEN THE TWO MOX SUMMITS, gained by traversing east beneath the western peak's southern side and then climbing a steep thousand feet of loose sandy talus.

THE HIGH CAMP'S OWN MARKER IS THAT IT SITS ON ROCK OUTCROPS AT THE GLACIER'S EDGE at the top of a broken buttress, rather than on open ice. Rope up there for the crevassed travel beyond; visibility on this ground is often poor, and the saddle is not visible from camp.

AT THE SADDLE, THE SUMMIT YOU WANT IS THE EASTERN ONE - the higher and harder of the pair. The western summit is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, so if the tower above you is on the side you came from, you have turned the wrong way.

THE CONFIRMATION SEQUENCE IS THE SAME LADDER: ramp right past a snow patch into a gully, class 4 up and right to a notch in the gendarme ridge, ledges zig-zagging right-left-right through it, then a short DOWNCLIMB to a small flat area, and only then the gully to the high notch on the west ridge where the rope comes out.
