backups.overview: The Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir ('CJ Couloir'), followed by Johannesburg's East Ridge, is the mountain's original and most-climbed line — first climbed July 26, 1938 by Calder Bressler, Bill Cox, Ray Clough, and Tom Myers. It also has one of the shortest approaches of any major North Cascades alpine route, but the couloir itself is the most direct and objectively dangerous way up the peak: a sustained roughly 3,400 ft gully of continuous 30-50° snow squeezed by the Sill Glacier, which threatens the lower two-thirds with icefall and opens dangerous, increasingly unbridged crevasses as the season progresses. Above the Cascade-Johannesburg col (~6,760 ft), about 1,400 ft of exposed, loose, mossy/broken-gneiss ridge — with rock pitches, gullies, ribs, and a knife-edge traverse up to low 5th class — leads to the summit.
backups.beta: First climbed July 26, 1938 by Calder Bressler, Bill Cox, Ray Clough and Tom Myers during the Ptarmigan Traverse — still the standard/easiest way up Johannesburg, though it is a serious glacier/couloir climb, not a walk-up. The couloir ascends 30-50° with a tight, crevassed bottleneck and an occasional water-ice step (AI2); above the col, the East Ridge follows a mossy, broken gneiss rib/gully system with a knife-edge traverse to the summit.
backups.turnaround: Because couloir conditions deteriorate quickly through the day, most successful parties start well before dawn (roughly 2-3am) to be through the couloir and back over the col by mid-morning; even for capable parties this is typically a 14-16 hour car-to-car day.
backups.rappels: 2-3 rappels (60m) down the East Ridge/east gully to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, using established anchors/slings
backups.face: Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir (Sill Glacier) to the East Ridge
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage on-route or at the trailhead; North Cascades NP advises climbers to be self-sufficient rather than rely on personal locator/cell devices for rescue.
backups.descent: Most parties reverse the East Ridge and downclimb/rappel the couloir back toward the trailhead; as the day warms, softening snow bridges over the Sill Glacier's crevasses, wet-slide activity, and rockfall in the couloir all increase sharply, so plan to be off the couloir by mid-morning. Some parties instead exit via the 'Doug's Direct' traverse from the C-J col (beneath the Triplets and over Mixup Peak's north ridge to the Cache Glacier and Cascade Pass) to avoid re-descending the couloir once conditions have deteriorated.

waypoints.directions: Follow Cascade River Road to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead, about 3,600 ft. In a heavy snow year the road can be gated well below the trailhead — one party found it gated at mile 18 with the road snow-free above to the last hairpin, and biked that section — so budget for the possibility rather than assuming you can drive to the end. Before you leave the car, look up: the couloir is the obvious deep gash between Cascade Peak on the left and Johannesburg on the right, in full view from the parking lot and the last road switchbacks. Judge whether the snow is continuous from here, in daylight, and be willing to turn around at the car.

backups.detailed_rack: Ice axe, a useful second tool for the steeper snow, crampons, a couple of pickets, a rope, and a helmet. No rock gear is generally needed beyond a few slings on the ridge.
pro_tips: Climb in a firm spring window with a stable snowpack.

Budget plenty of time for the long east ridge.

backups.pro_needs: Protection is limited to pickets in the couloir and the occasional sling on the ridge. This is a steep-snow and endurance route where conditions and timing matter more than gear.
backups.best_season: Late April through June, before the Sill Glacier's crevasses open; by mid-to-late summer the couloir is generally considered unsafe as an early-season-only line, though some parties still climb it into September with more technical difficulty (an AI2 ice step has been reported low in the couloir late-season).
backups.approach: Shares its start with the Northeast Buttress: from the Cascade Pass trailhead (~3,600 ft), descend briefly from the parking lot, cross the creek/river drainage, and work through brush and a terminal moraine to reach a permanent snowfield around 3,300 ft. It's one of the more compact approaches in the range, but the brush travel is unpleasant in the dark on an alpine-start day.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the east ridge and descend the couloir, ideally while the snow remains firm, watching for rockfall and slide activity as the day warms.
backups.bail: Retreat by downclimbing the couloir is feasible if conditions are still good, but the steep snow and rockfall make a late or warm-conditions descent hazardous, so timing the climb to allow a firm-snow retreat is important.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb from the avalanche-debris fan into the couloir, which is walled by rock on both sides and overhung by the Sill Glacier serac on the Johannesburg side. Rock and ice come down as the sun reaches the walls, so be moving early on firm snow. Crevasses and snow-to-rock steps appear as the season goes on.

The couloir narrows into a choke, often scoured by meltwater from the summits above and carrying a bulge of water ice that may need a belay and a screw or two. A narrower looker's-right line sometimes goes cleanly around it. There is no shelter here from falling debris: do not stop in the choke.

Above the choke, go up and left, then straight up the final couloir to the Cascade-Johannesburg col (about 6,760 ft). In mid- to late season the snow turns discontinuous, with bergschrunds and near-vertical steps; early season is the sensible window. A cornice can span the col, and a way around it has been found against the rock of Cascade Peak on the left.

From the col, climb the steep east side on heather, talus and broken rock bands, mostly Class 3-4. Steep heather here is harder to protect than it looks. Pass rock horns on the shoulder to a red dike, then climb a steep gray gully of about 500 ft to the false summit (about 8,040 ft). Its top has a couple of options, one with low-5th moves.

From the false summit, drop about 30 ft and traverse south-side ledges roughly 75 ft below the crest, working in and out of many loose ribs and gullies with constant exposure. In cloud this ground is easy to get lost on. A deep slot-gully gives one final Class 3-4 pitch to the true summit. A small bivy site lies not far below the top.

itinerary.cal: The couloir climbs best on firm snow well before dawn from late April through June; as the day warms, softening snow bridges over the Sill Glacier and wet-slide/rockfall risk both rise, which is why parties race to be off it by mid-day.

days.note: Hike the Cascade Pass trail then cut cross-country toward Cascade-Johannesburg col, gaining the flanks below the couloir. Most parties reach a flat bivy spot near the col with time to rest before an alpine-start next morning.

days.note: An alpine-start ascent of the snow couloir onto the ridge crest, then sustained, loose, exposed 3rd-5th class climbing along the East Ridge to the true summit. The whole route is then downclimbed/rappelled and the couloir descended before it softens, followed by the long hike out — real parties report finishing well after dark.

access.fees: No park entrance fee — North Cascades NP is fee-free. Summer-season backcountry permits (mid-May through early October) cost $10/person/night plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee; free outside that window.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: No permit is required for a single-day climb; an overnight bivy or any backcountry camping requires a North Cascades NP wilderness/backcountry permit, reservable on Recreation.gov or obtained walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
access.permit: North Cascades NP wilderness/backcountry camping permit (required for any overnight stay; day climbs need none)
access.closures: Cascade River Road is gated for winter at the park boundary (milepost 18) and typically doesn't reopen to the Cascade Pass trailhead until late June, sometimes not until early July in heavy-snow years — this matters for this route's late-April/May target season, since the trailhead itself may still be inaccessible by vehicle.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (South Unit), National Park Service
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: None for day climbing; a wilderness permit (not a parking pass) is only needed if bivying overnight.

overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center up to a day ahead.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Paved for the first ~10 miles out of Marblemount, then rough gravel; the final ~3 miles to the Cascade Pass trailhead are narrow with steep drop-offs. Trailers and vehicles over 22 ft long / 8 ft wide are prohibited within the park boundary.
road.driveNote: 23.1 miles from SR 20 in Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead when open, about an hour's drive.
road.seasonalGate: Gated at the park boundary (mile 18) in winter; foot and bike travel is allowed beyond the gate when closed to vehicles. Typically reopens to the Cascade Pass trailhead by late June, occasionally not until early July — early-season (April/May) CJ Couloir parties should check current status, as they may need to walk or bike the final miles.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone — daily NWAC avalanche forecasts run mid-November through mid-April, so for the typical late-April–June climbing window rely on recent trip reports and NPS road and trail condition updates once the regular forecast season ends.

emergency.notes: North Cascades NP SAR typically builds in an extra day before initiating a search for overdue Johannesburg climbers, given the mountain's reputation for long, complex descents.
emergency.rangerStation: Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, North Cascades National Park, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA 98267, (360) 854-7245

crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - a well-known objective among North Cascades ski/snow climbers but with a short, weather-dependent window; overall the mountain reportedly sees only a handful of ascents per year across all routes, so the CJ Couloir likely sees a similarly small number of parties per season

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Serious: a confined couloir with avalanche and rockfall runout, sustained steep snow with limited protection, a long route-finding ridge, and wet slides on the descent as the day warms

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass trailhead to the couloir apron
approach_variants.notes:
Effectively no approach at all. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft, walk back down the road — accounts range from a quarter mile to just under a mile depending on where you drop in — then descend a dirt and brush embankment into the valley and cross the Cascade River. In spring the river is often still snow-covered where you cross.

Over the terminal moraine and a snowfield, and within about twenty minutes of dropping off the road you are putting crampons on at the apron at roughly 3,300 ft. From there it is about 3,000 ft of continuous booting to the Cascade-Johannesburg col.

In a big snow year Cascade River Road may be gated well below the trailhead — one ski party found it gated at mile 18 but snow-free to the last hairpin, and used bikes for the road section. Budget for that possibility rather than assuming you can drive to the end.

Season is the whole decision on this route. Early season is when the snow is continuous. As the Sill Glacier breaks up, the snow in the couloir goes discontinuous where it narrows near the hanging glacier and the breaks turn into a series of separate problems; by mid to late summer it is broken and considerably more hazardous.
approach_variants.season: May-Jun, while the Sill Glacier snow is still continuous
hazards: Rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier over the whole couloir
Discontinuous snow where the couloir narrows, worsening through the season
Cascade River crossing — snow-bridged in spring, a ford later
Spring wet-slide activity in a 3,000 ft snow chute
Road may be gated miles below the trailhead in a heavy snow year
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is easy to find and the hard part is judging it, which is unusual on this list. The couloir is the obvious deep gash in the skyline directly between Cascade Peak on the left and Johannesburg on the right, and it is in full view from the trailhead parking lot and the last road switchbacks. Identify it from the car, in daylight, before you drop into the valley — this is the one approach here where you get a complete view of your line before committing to it, and you should use that. On the ground, you are at the base when the moraine and brush end and you step onto a continuous snow apron at around 3,300 ft. From the apron, looking up the couloir, the line is unambiguous — there are no alternative gullies to confuse it with. What you cannot see from the apron is the part that matters. The couloir narrows higher up near the obvious hanging glacier, and that is where the snow goes discontinuous as the season progresses. A base that looks perfect in July tells you nothing about the middle. Judge continuity from the road, where the whole 3,000 ft is in view, and be willing to turn around at the car. The honest caveat carried by every source that describes this line: it is the most direct route on Johannesburg and also the most dangerous, guarded by overhead rock and ice fall that is hard to justify once the snow is not continuous.

bivy.name: Cascade-Johannesburg Col bivy
bivy.notes: Top of the CJ Couloir between Cascade Peak and Johannesburg. Most parties sleep here and climb to the summit the next morning.
bivy.water: Snow at the col; running water on the bench below early in the season
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP wilderness permit required
bivy.capacity: A few small bivy sites at the col and on the heather bench below it

bivy.name: Johannesburg Camp
bivy.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
bivy.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.
